hook: You know Jeremiah 29:11. But did you know it was written to exiles who had just been told to settle in for seventy years?
story:
Picture the people who first heard these words. They had seen their king taken away. They had been marched from their homes to Babylon, the capital of the empire that had conquered them. Every one of them was asking the same question: how long?

Back in Jerusalem a prophet named Hananiah had an answer everyone wanted. In the temple, in front of the crowd, he took the wooden bar Jeremiah wore on his neck as a sign of Babylon’s rule, and broke it. “Within two full years”, he promised, it would all be over.

Jeremiah had to say what nobody wanted to hear: “The LORD has not sent you, but you make this people trust in a lie.” Before the year was out, Hananiah was dead.

Then comes the letter. Not two years. Seventy. Long enough that many who heard it read aloud would never see home again. And it is to them that God says he thinks thoughts of peace, “to give you hope and a future”.
moment:
The speaker is God, and his words reach the exiles in a letter. Jeremiah wrote it in Jerusalem and sent it to Babylon, addressed to the elders, the priests, the prophets and “all the people whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away captive”.

Imagine it being read aloud to them. They are waiting to hear that they can go home. The letter begins with almost the opposite: “Build houses and dwell in them. Plant gardens and eat their fruit.” Marry. Have children. Pray for the city that holds you captive, “for in its peace you will have peace”. Settle in. This will take a long time.
around: The verse before it sets the time: “After seventy years are accomplished for Babylon, I will visit you”. The verses after it promise that the people will call and pray and be heard, and that God will bring them back.
readings:
For Jewish readers this is first of all a promise kept. The exile did end, and the people did come home.

Christians have read it in more than one way. Many take it personally: the God who had plans for the exiles has plans for each of his children. Others point out that the promise was made to a whole people, at one moment in their history, and that it took seventy years to come true. They read it as a window into the character of God, who does not forget his people even when the waiting is long.

The two readings do not have to fight. The first is at its truest when it remembers the second: the hope is certain, and it may not be quick.
point: The hope is real, and it is slow. Seventy years is a lifetime. The promise is given to a people in exile, and it comes with an instruction to live faithfully where they are in the meantime.
